video_title: Scaling Laws: Building AI Assurance Ecosystem
gist: Bree (executive director of the newly launched PACT AI — Partnership for Assurance, Credibility, and Trust on AI) and Rob of UL Solutions argue that the missing layer in AI governance is a third-party assurance ecosystem serving deployers, not just frontier developers, and size that emerging market at hundreds of billions of dollars. They detail PACT AI's 90-day founding sprint and three committees, UL's new UL 3115 AI product-safety standard (~200 parameters, first two certifications were software), and the core technical problem: certification regimes built for deterministic products must now handle over-the-air updates, single-system drift, and multi-agent emergent behavior. The recurring bottleneck is data access from developers, and the recurring commercial claim is that unresolved liability is capping enterprise AI adoption.

insights.claim: PACT AI — the Partnership for Assurance, Credibility, and Trust on AI — launched as a multi-stakeholder body convening enterprises, independent technical evaluators, AI insurers, and civil society to build 'whole economy infrastructure' for verifying that AI systems work as intended.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: A new industry body with insurer participation is the clearest early signal of where AI liability pricing and enterprise procurement standards will be set; watch its membership roster as a proxy for which vendors will face third-party audit requirements first.
insights.quote: we have AI insurers, those folks who are trying to figure out how do we underwrite this?

insights.claim: PACT AI's executive director estimates the emerging AI assurance ecosystem will be worth upwards of hundreds of billions of dollars in the coming years, framing verification and evaluation as a genuinely new market rather than a compliance cost center.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: Sizes a whitespace market for testing, evaluation, audit, and certification providers — relevant to anyone underwriting TIC (testing/inspection/certification) incumbents or AI-eval startups.
insights.quote: There are estimates that this AI assurance ecosystem will be upwards of, you know, hundreds of billions of dollars in the coming years.

insights.claim: PACT AI ran a 90-day founding sprint and emerged with three committees — policy, AI assurance (infrastructure), and market development — operating deliberately like a conventional trade association where members vote on priorities and lead working groups.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: The trade-association structure tells you output cadence and where influence sits; the market development committee is the one that would actually move procurement dollars toward assurance vendors.

insights.claim: PACT AI's near-term commercial thesis is intermediation — 'getting the pipes to line up' between enterprises that need answers and the technical providers who can generate them — because the binding constraint is awareness and connection, not the absence of capability.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: If matching, not capability, is the gap, the fastest-monetizing layer is distribution/marketplace for evaluation services rather than novel eval science.
insights.quote: We call it getting the pipes to line up more quickly.

themes.theme: The deployer bottleneck and duplicated evaluation cost

insights.claim: AI governance discourse concentrates on frontier developers and end users while neglecting deployers — the companies and nonprofits that integrate AI into operations — and that neglect is itself slowing safe diffusion because no one can say who is on the hook when harm occurs.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: The deployer tier is the under-served customer segment in AI governance tooling — a market gap for indemnification, certification, and audit products aimed at enterprise integrators rather than model builders.
insights.quote: you can outsource a task to AI, but you can't outsource the accountability

insights.claim: Every health system independently evaluating the same vendor model duplicates identical work with non-transferable methods, which prices AI evaluation out of reach for any organization without an in-house data science team — per Denver Health's head of AI.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI), quoting Dr. Khorsh of Denver Health
insights.so_what: A textbook case for shared-infrastructure economics: whoever builds transferable model evaluations for regulated verticals captures the redundant spend, and small deployers are the underserved buyer.
insights.quote: every health system evaluating the same vendor model is doing that work alone with its own methods and the result doesn't transfer to anyone else

insights.claim: Large multinationals describe having to 'boil the ocean' on every internal AI deployment because covering all evaluation ground themselves is the only way to get comfortable — an inefficiency that advantages firms willing to skip the diligence entirely.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI), quoting an unnamed multinational
insights.so_what: Absent shared assurance, the fastest AI adopters are the least careful ones — an adverse-selection dynamic that raises tail risk in enterprise AI deployments and eventual insurance losses.
insights.quote: Every time I want to use AI we have to boil the ocean because the only way for us to feel good about this is to cover all of every ground and it's incredibly inefficient.

insights.claim: Contrary to the common view that assurance slows deployment, PACT AI's position is that at the current adoption stage assurance is an accelerant — without it the rollout will be 'jagged', opaque, and slower than needed.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: Reframes assurance spend as a growth investment rather than compliance drag — the pitch enterprise buyers will hear, and the argument that determines whether the market reaches the hundreds-of-billions estimate.
insights.quote: I think that often people think of assurance as slowing down or a cost. In the moment we are right now, it is going to be an expediter for how we do this well and responsibly.

insights.claim: An executive at a financial institution told PACT AI's director point-blank that the firm can only take AI so far until liability is sorted out — an explicit statement that unresolved legal exposure, not model capability, is the current adoption ceiling in regulated finance.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI), quoting a financial-institution executive
insights.so_what: Direct read on why enterprise AI revenue in regulated sectors lags pilot activity — liability resolution, not model quality, is the unlock to watch for financial-sector AI spend.
insights.quote: we're only going to be able to take AI so far until liability gets sorted out here

themes.theme: Why assurance can't stop at the frontier lab

insights.claim: PACT AI rejects the framing that pushing more testing and liability onto Anthropic and OpenAI is the simpler fix: assurance is needed from pre-deployment through downstream deployment into water systems, schools, and hospitals, because frontier checks don't cover context-specific application behavior.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: Implies regulatory and audit obligations propagate down the value chain to deployers and integrators, not just model providers — expanding the addressable base for compliance tooling well beyond a handful of labs.

insights.claim: The billions and trillions of dollars invested at the AI frontier create momentum that by default puts decision-making power with model developers, which is the structural argument for building independent verification capacity now rather than after norms harden.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: Capital concentration as a governance variable — the same capex wave that drives AI infrastructure returns also determines who writes the safety norms, a factor for anyone modeling regulatory risk to lab valuations.

insights.claim: UL Solutions frames third-party assurance as additive rather than substitutive — it adds evidence and accountability without removing developer or deployer responsibility — and argues too many incentives are involved to rely on developers to self-report failures.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Positions certification as layered on top of, not in place of, liability — meaning assurance spend is incremental to legal and insurance costs rather than offsetting them.
insights.quote: There are too many incentives involved to just rely on the developer themselves to catch that.

insights.claim: Traditional assurance presumes deterministic products — same inputs, same outputs, 100 times out of 100 — and AI fails on all three counts, which is the fundamental methodological problem facing every certification body entering the space.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host), citing Dr. Ned Carney of Mount Sinai
insights.so_what: The core technical risk in the AI-certification thesis: if determinism-based methods don't transfer, incumbent TIC firms' 130-year moats may be weaker in AI than their brand suggests.
insights.quote: traditional assurance works for deterministic products

insights.claim: UL Solutions decomposes AI's dynamism into three distinct assurance problems: planned over-the-air updates, unplanned single-system drift or hallucination, and multi-agent emergent behavior — with only the first resembling anything the certification industry has handled before.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: A usable taxonomy for evaluating any AI monitoring or assurance vendor — ask which of the three it actually covers; most tooling today addresses only the first two.

insights.claim: UL Solutions cites 'mind viruses' — a term it attributes to Anthropic — for cases where a group of AI systems or agents together shifts behavior in unexpected ways, and treats this plurality failure mode as newly urgent following a recent high-profile incident.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Multi-agent emergent failure is now entering formal certification vocabulary — an early indicator that agentic deployments will attract audit requirements ahead of single-model ones.
insights.quote: the most recent and it's what I believe Anthropic uh coined the term mind viruses

insights.claim: The operative certification test for dynamic AI becomes envelope-based — whether a system has drifted outside a safety envelope the ecosystem defined — which converts certification from a one-time pass into a continuous monitoring service with defined triggers for pulling the mark.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Turns a one-off certification fee into recurring revenue — the business-model shift that makes AI assurance structurally more attractive than legacy product testing.
insights.quote: Did it go outside the envelope or did it not? That's a dynamic type of a performance parameter

insights.claim: Both PACT AI and UL Solutions identify data access from model developers as the binding constraint on the entire assurance model, because without a recurring flow of performance data any certification label goes stale.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI) and Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Watch whether frontier labs actually sign data-sharing agreements with assurance bodies — that is the single gating event for the assurance market to become real rather than nominal.
insights.quote: It's not sufficient for the long term because of that dynamism

themes.theme: UL 3115 and the mechanics of the certification business

insights.claim: UL Solutions' UL 3115 standard for AI-based product safety covers technical, ethical, and governance pillars across roughly 200 parameters, with accountability — who built it, how it was trained, bias and transparency — the pillar most recently strengthened.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-live AI certification standard that enterprise buyers can demand today — the nearest thing to a shipping product in the AI assurance market.
insights.quote: It covers technical, ethical, and governance pillars. The one that we beefed up most recently is actually accountability.

insights.claim: UL Solutions' first two UL 3115 certifications were software rather than physical products — an AI battery management system and an AI building management system — a departure from its 132-year hardware history, with AI-enabled smoke detectors, control panels, and laptops now following.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Demand is arriving first in industrial and building-systems AI, not consumer or frontier applications — a directional read on where AI certification revenue actually lands early.
insights.quote: our first two certifications through were not physical products. Um, they were software.

insights.claim: An assurance provider's franchise rests on three commitments — impartiality, consistency, and competency — with impartiality enforced by never advising on design: failed products get a scorecard, not a remediation plan, because telling a customer how to fix it makes the assessor a designer.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: A test to apply to any AI-eval vendor pitching both consulting and certification — the combination breaks the impartiality that gives a mark its value.
insights.quote: we don't tell customers how to redesign a product because that makes us a designer

insights.claim: Competency is the hardest of the three commitments for AI because engineers graduating five years ago had no AI skills in their curriculum, forcing UL Solutions to retrain a 15,000-person workforce to assess AI-enabled products credibly.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Assurance capacity is talent-constrained, not demand-constrained — a governor on how fast the certification market can scale, and a hiring-cost headwind for incumbent TIC firms.
insights.quote: Engineers 5 years ago were not graduating with AI skills baked in

insights.claim: UL Solutions' surveillance model — unannounced factory visits pulling production samples on a predictable annual cadence for retest — is the template it intends to carry into AI, replacing physical pulls with periodic performance checks keyed to each product's refresh rate.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: The operational blueprint for continuous AI certification; whether developers grant the equivalent 'unannounced pull' access to live model behavior determines if the analogy holds.
insights.quote: we will go unannounced and we will collect product from the the factory

themes.theme: Race-to-the-bottom, capture risk, and the enforcement backstop

insights.claim: The defense against certification arbitrage — a lax competitor issuing a confusingly similar mark — is consensus standards rather than litigation: a one-off private bar is visibly not consensus, and consensus processes tend to self-police.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Consensus-standard participation, not mark ownership, is the durable moat in assurance — which favors bodies embedded in standards-setting over standalone AI-audit startups.
insights.quote: it's not consensus, it's your one-off versus a PACT AI or an ecosystem that has been set through balanced consensus

insights.claim: UL structurally separates standard-setting from certification — the sister organization UL Standards and Engagement governs the standards and balances technical committees so UL Solutions holds one and only one vote — and PACT AI has adopted an analogous governance design to blunt capture by large members.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions) and Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: The governance separation is what large deployers will scrutinize before treating a mark as credible; its absence in a competing scheme is a red flag.
insights.quote: They balance those technical committees so that we get one and only one vote.

insights.claim: UL Solutions is building AI assurance on the explicit assumption of a voluntary regime — regulation helps but is not required — while PACT AI's director argues government intervention will ultimately be needed both to legitimize the assurance system and to hold it accountable for producing better outcomes.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions) and Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: A near-term voluntary market with an expected regulatory backstop is the most favorable setup for assurance providers — revenue now, mandated demand later.
insights.quote: we're going to need some kind of government intervention here, most likely

insights.claim: The single most tractable near-term gap is the demand signal, which is currently lost in taxonomy: enterprises don't know what to ask AI developers for, and imprecise asks die in procurement and legal review — 'ships passing in the night'.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: Standardized procurement language for AI assurance is the lowest-cost, highest-leverage intervention — and the first place a startup or standards body can create defensible position.
insights.quote: The employers don't necessarily know what to ask of developers. They don't have the right language and then it gets moved through procurement and legal teams

insights.claim: PACT AI's mapping work identified over 200 organizations already doing AI assurance science and technology, which its director says puts the field in a better position than the prevailing zeitgeist suggests — the deficit is coordination and pace, not raw supply.
insights.speaker: Bree (executive director, PACT AI)
insights.so_what: A fragmented 200+ vendor landscape with no coordination layer is a consolidation and roll-up setup, and evidence the constraint is distribution rather than technology.
insights.quote: we have over 200 organizations that are doing this science and technology

insights.claim: UL Solutions points to social media's path — no accountability attached to how algorithms were wired, ending in verdicts of roughly $18 billion — as the fresh cautionary lesson driving current enterprise demand for AI assurance.
insights.speaker: Rob (UL Solutions)
insights.so_what: Litigation outcomes in adjacent sectors are functioning as the demand generator for AI certification — escalating social-media damages should be read as a leading indicator for AI assurance spend.
insights.quote: we don't want to have that kind of a very difficult path, slow path that results in, you know, $18 billion verdicts out there

insights.claim: Existing unfair-and-deceptive-acts statutes already let state attorneys general prosecute products that don't match claimed specifications, so third-party certification makes current law more enforceable without waiting for new AI legislation.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Certification claims create enforceable representations — meaning the legal exposure from a stale or overstated AI mark arrives via state AGs long before any federal AI statute does.
insights.quote: if you release a product that doesn't align with the specifications you claim it does, that's illegal and we can come after you
